claim: Ras-superfamily GTPases are central controllers of cell proliferation and morphology.
source: The Ras-superfamily GTPases are central controllers of cell proliferation and morphology.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on Ras GTPase functions in cell proliferation and morphology.

claim: Ras signaling is mediated by a system of interacting molecules including upstream enzymes (GEF/GAP) that regulate Ras's ability to recruit multiple competing downstream effectors.
source: Ras signaling is mediated by a system of interacting molecules: upstream enzymes (GEF/GAP) regulate Ras's ability to recruit multiple competing downstream effectors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Ras signaling architecture.

claim: The concentration and identity of both upstream and downstream signaling components strongly impacted the timing, duration, shape, and amplitude of effector outputs.
source: The concentration and identity of both upstream and downstream signaling components strongly impacted the timing, duration, shape, and amplitude of effector outputs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing how varying component concentrations affects output dynamics.

claim: The distorted output of oncogenic alleles of Ras was highly dependent on the balance of positive (GAP) and negative (GEF) regulators in the system.
source: The distorted output of oncogenic alleles of Ras was highly dependent on the balance of positive (GAP) and negative (GEF) regulators in the system.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing wild-type and oncogenic Ras under different GAP/GEF conditions.

claim: Different effectors interpreted the same inputs with distinct output dynamics, enabling a Ras system to encode multiple unique temporal outputs in response to a single input.
source: We found that different effectors interpreted the same inputs with distinct output dynamics, enabling a Ras system to encode multiple unique temporal outputs in response to a single input.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing different effector responses to the same Ras activation.

claim: Different Ras-to-GEF positive feedback mechanisms could reshape output dynamics in distinct ways, such as signal amplification or overshoot minimization.
source: We also found that different Ras-to-GEF positive feedback mechanisms could reshape output dynamics in distinct ways, such as signal amplification or overshoot minimization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different feedback mechanisms.

claim: Mutations in Ras superfamily GTPases are often associated with cancer or other diseases.
source: Mutations in these important molecules are often associated with cancer or other diseases (Bos, 1989; Schubbert et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on Ras mutations in disease.

claim: Small GTPases act as macromolecular 'switches' at cell membranes, cycling between an ON state when bound to GTP and an OFF state when bound to GDP.
source: These small GTPases act as macromolecular 'switches' at cell membranes, cycling between an ON state when bound to GTP and an OFF state when bound to GDP (Bourne et al., 1990) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and supported by citation and Figure 1A.

claim: Only the GTP-bound state of Ras is able to interact with downstream effector molecules and assemble signaling complexes.
source: This notion of an ON and OFF state of the GTPase is manifest in differences in the conformation of the protein such that, in most cases, only the GTP-bound state is able to interact with downstream effector molecules and assemble signaling complexes (Krengel et al., 1990; Milburn et al., 1990; Nassar et al., 1995; Herrmann, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Ras GTPases are incredibly slow at each stage of the catalytic cycle except for the initial binding of nucleotide.
source: As enzymes, these GTPases are formally capable of binding GTP, hydrolyzing it to GDP+Pi, and releasing product to complete the catalytic cycle on their own, but, in practice, the GTPase is incredibly slow at each stage of this cycle except for the initial binding of nucleotide (Neal et al., 1988; Gibbs et al., 1984; McGrath et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to kinetic studies of Ras.

claim: Guanine exchange factors (GEFs) promote product release by emptying the nucleotide pocket of the GTPase and allowing subsequent reloading of the GTPase with nucleotide (OFF->ON transition).
source: As such, molecules that can accelerate these slow steps in the catalytic cycle function as essential regulators of GTPase activity during signaling events: guanine exchange factors (GEFs), which promote product release by emptying the nucleotide pocket of the GTPase and allowing subsequent reloading of the GTPase with nucleotide (OFF->ON transition); and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) which accelerate the hydrolysis of GTP to GDP+Pi (ON->OFF transition) (Figure 1A) (Boguski and McCormick, 1993; Trahey and McCormick, 1987; Bos et al., 2007; McCormick et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the mechanism.

claim: GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) accelerate the hydrolysis of GTP to GDP+Pi (ON->OFF transition).
source: As such, molecules that can accelerate these slow steps in the catalytic cycle function as essential regulators of GTPase activity during signaling events: guanine exchange factors (GEFs), which promote product release by emptying the nucleotide pocket of the GTPase and allowing subsequent reloading of the GTPase with nucleotide (OFF->ON transition); and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) which accelerate the hydrolysis of GTP to GDP+Pi (ON->OFF transition) (Figure 1A) (Boguski and McCormick, 1993; Trahey and McCormick, 1987; Bos et al., 2007; McCormick et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the mechanism.

claim: GEF assays typically monitor a single exchange of fluorescent nucleotide for non-fluorescent nucleotide.
source: To study the regulators, however, these reconstitutions are almost always performed under conditions in which Ras cannot productively cycle: GEF assays monitor a single exchange of fluorescent nucleotide for non-fluorescent nucleotide; GAP assays monitor a single turnover of GTP without the possibility of the nucleotide reloading (Eberth and Ahmadian, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to methods literature.

claim: GAP assays typically monitor a single turnover of GTP without the possibility of the nucleotide reloading.
source: To study the regulators, however, these reconstitutions are almost always performed under conditions in which Ras cannot productively cycle: GEF assays monitor a single exchange of fluorescent nucleotide for non-fluorescent nucleotide; GAP assays monitor a single turnover of GTP without the possibility of the nucleotide reloading (Eberth and Ahmadian, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to methods literature.

claim: Studies of effector interactions with activated GTPase are typically done under non-cycling conditions using non-hydrolyzable nucleotide analogs to measure equilibrium binding constants.
source: Likewise, studies of effector interactions with activated GTPase are typically done under non-cycling conditions using non-hydrolyzable nucleotide analogs to measure equilibrium binding constants (Geyer, 1996; Herrmann et al., 1996; Sydor et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: Signaling dynamics are critical for many cellular responses.
source: However, we know that signaling dynamics are critical for many cellular responses, and yet these features have not been analyzed in most in vitro studies of Ras signaling.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in cell signaling.

claim: The authors developed a microscopy-based bead reconstitution assay of dynamic signal processing by human H-Ras.
source: Here, to address this problem of systems reconstitution, we develop a new microscopy-based bead reconstitution assay of dynamic signal processing by human H-Ras, a canonical member of the Ras subfamily of GTPases.
evidence: This describes the experimental method developed in this study.

claim: The reconstitution system includes both upstream regulators of Ras activity as well as multiple downstream effectors that bind to and perceive Ras•GTP signals.
source: Our system includes both upstream regulators of Ras activity as well as multiple downstream effectors that bind to and perceive Ras•GTP signals.
evidence: This describes the components of the experimental system.

claim: The system allows tracking of multiple cycles of Ras turnover in real-time using the bead recruitment of fluorescently tagged effectors on Ras as the measured output.
source: This allows us to follow multiple cycles of Ras turnover in real-time using the bead recruitment of fluorescently tagged effectors on Ras as the measured output – precisely analogous to the way cells measure and couple Ras•GTP levels to signaling outputs.
evidence: This describes the measurement approach in the experimental system.

claim: A microsphere surface charged with Ras can serve as a platform for the assembly and disassembly of fluorescent effector molecules from solution in response to inputs.
source: We reasoned that a microsphere surface charged with Ras could serve as a platform for the assembly and disassembly of fluorescent effector molecules from solution in response to inputs, much like the native Ras system (bound to the plasma membrane) functions in cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental design, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: GEF-catalyzed GTP-dependent translocation of fluorescent effector to Ras-loaded beads was observed.
source: Upon GEF and nucleotide addition, there was noticeable accumulation of fluorescent effector on the bead surface of the GTP containing reactions within seconds, and considerable fluorescent signal was observed by 10 min. In contrast, no fluorescent effector accumulated on the surface of reactions containing GDP, indicating that GEF-catalyzed translocation of the effector was dependent on Ras becoming GTP loaded.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of GEF stimulated assembly of effector on the bead as the levels of Ras•GTP increased.
source: As before, addition of GEF stimulated assembly of effector on the bead as the levels of Ras•GTP increased.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: When NF1-GAP was added to the reactions, the system responded with a rapid decrease in effector levels before stabilizing at a non-zero plateau corresponding to the non-equilibrium steady state maintained by the balance of effector, GEF and GAP activities present in the reaction.
source: When NF1-GAP was added to the reactions, the system responded with a rapid decrease in effector levels before stabilizing at a non-zero plateau corresponding to the non-equilibrium steady state maintained by the balance of effector, GEF and GAP activities present in the reaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Oncogenic mutations of Ras (especially at the G12, G13, or Q61 positions) are frequently associated with cancer or other diseases.
source: Mutations of Ras (especially at the G12, G13, or Q61 positions) are frequently associated with cancer or other diseases (Barbacid, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Oncogenic Ras alleles impact Ras signaling through three mechanisms: decreasing the intrinsic hydrolysis rate of the GTPase, blocking GAP-mediated hydrolysis of the GTPase, and potentially altering the interaction and preference of the GTPase for downstream effectors.
source: These alleles are primarily thought to impact Ras signaling through three mechanisms: 1) decreasing the intrinsic hydrolysis rate of the GTPase, 2) blocking GAP-mediated hydrolysis of the GTPase, and 3) potentially altering the interaction and preference of the GTPase for downstream effectors (Figure 3A) (Trahey and McCormick, 1987; Barbacid, 1987; Rajalingam et al., 2007; Smith and Ikura, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 3A illustrating the mechanisms.

claim: Wild type and G12V Ras systems produced very similar outputs with almost no difference in the total integrated effector output in GAP-free network configurations.
source: Under this network configuration, wild type and G12V Ras systems produced very similar outputs with almost no difference in the total integrated effector output and only small differences in the overall dynamics of their responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In networks that included 1 μM basal NF1-GAP, both the dynamics and amplitude of the effector output were substantially distorted by the Ras-G12V allele.
source: Unlike in the GEF-only networks, both the dynamics and amplitude of the effector output were substantially distorted by the Ras-G12V allele.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Wild-type Ras produced a transient response that peaked within an hour and declined to a steady state less than 20% its maximum value in high-GAP networks.
source: In this network configuration, wild-type Ras produced a transient response that peaked within an hour and declined to a steady state less than 20% its maximum value.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: G12V Ras outputs were sustained and increased in magnitude for over 6 hr before settling at a steady state more than 40 times higher than wild-type Ras in high-GAP networks.
source: In contrast, outputs from G12V were sustained and increased in magnitude for over 6 hr before settling at a steady state more than 40 times higher than wild-type Ras.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: G12V alleles were most perturbative with low-GEF inputs and a high-GAP network context.
source: This revealed that G12V alleles were most perturbative with low-GEF inputs and a high-GAP network context, conditions in which the GAP activity would, for wild-type Ras, completely dominate over the small amount of activating GEF input.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Two-state systems cannot show overshoot behavior.
source: Indeed, this is consistent with analytic results that state that two-state systems cannot show overshoot behavior (Jia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Transient overshoot could be introduced into the system by two non-mutually exclusive mechanisms: competition between effectors and GAP molecules, and the existence of a post-hydrolysis GTPase state that is refractory to GEF stimulation.
source: However, transient overshoot could be easily introduced into the system by two non-mutually exclusive mechanisms: (1) competition between effectors and GAP molecules; and (2) the existence of a post-hydrolysis GTPase state that is refractory to GEF stimulation.
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The introduction of a refractory GTPase state to the model produced overshoot that captured the key features of the observed data within physiological parameters.
source: In contrast, the introduction of a refractory GTPase state to the model produced overshoot that captured the key features of the observed data within physiological parameters: a monotonic response to inputs in low-GAP networks but a transient response in high-GAP networks (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing levels of NF1-GAP resulted in substantially lower end point steady state levels of bound effector.
source: First, increasing levels of NF1-GAP resulted in substantially lower end point steady state levels of bound effector.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Networks containing NF1-GAP showed transient overshoot that decayed back down to the steady state from above, creating an initial pulse of strong output followed by weaker levels of output in the long term.
source: Moreover, the amount of NF1-GAP changed the dynamics of approach to steady state significantly: while GAP-free networks approached steady state from below, networks containing NF1-GAP showed transient overshoot that decayed back down to the steady state from above, creating an initial pulse of strong output followed by weaker levels of output in the long term.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The pulse-width and peak-time of effector outputs were inversely correlated with the concentration of the NF1-GAP.
source: The pulse-width and peak-time of effector outputs were inversely correlated with the concentration of the NF1-GAP (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The impact of the p120GAP on the end-point effector output of the system was much less substantial compared to NF1-GAP.
source: Compared to the NF1-GAP, the impact of the p120GAP on the end-point effector output of the system was much less substantial (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Ras density was directly correlated with the amplitude of effector output produced by the system.
source: Applying this approach to our fixed step-input, we found that the Ras density was directly correlated with the amplitude of effector output produced by the system (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At lower Ras densities, effector output responses were increasingly transient in character.
source: At lower Ras densities, however, effector output responses were increasingly transient in character.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Higher effector concentrations not only increase output amplitudes but also enable the output to capture more transient features of the upstream Ras•GTP signal.
source: These data demonstrate that higher effector concentrations not only increase output amplitudes but also enable the output to capture more transient features of the upstream Ras•GTP signal.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Effectors are not merely passive conduits for transmitting upstream Ras dynamics, but instead play an active role in interpreting and perceiving what features of those dynamics to pass downstream during signaling.
source: This implies that effectors are not merely passive conduits for transmitting upstream Ras dynamics, but instead play an active role in interpreting and perceiving what features of those dynamics to pass downstream during signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing effector concentration effects.

claim: Different effector molecules have different binding affinities that are determined by different on and off rates from the target, and thus will interpret Ras dynamics differently.
source: First, as we previously saw with one-effector systems, the time it takes for a binding process to equilibrate impacts the extent to which it can track the transient dynamics of its target. Distinct effector molecules have different binding affinities that are determined by different on and off rates from the target, and thus will interpret Ras dynamics differently.
evidence: This is based on inference from experimental observations and established biochemical principles.

claim: In GAP-free networks, C-Raf and B-Raf processed signals with different amplitudes and completely different dynamics.
source: In response to a 2 μM RasGRF GEF step input in a GAP-free network, C-Raf and B-Raf processed these signals with different amplitudes and completely different dynamics (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In high NF1-GAP network context, C-Raf output peaked within 30 min before sharply declining to a steady state value 25% of its maximum, while B-Raf output peaked later at 1 hr and declined to 75% its peak maximum.
source: When these step-responses were re-examined in a high NF1-GAP network context, we continued to see different effector responses between C-Raf and B-Raf: C-Raf output peaked within 30 min before sharply declining to a steady state value 25% of its maximum. In contrast, B-Raf output peaked later at 1 hr, and declined to a 75% its peak maximum, a much higher steady state compared to C-Raf (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A single-step input can be used to encode multiple classes of temporally distinct outputs that peak and decline out of phase with one another, allowing for a sequence of different activities to be organized during signal processing.
source: Consequently, a single-step input can be in principle be used encode multiple classes of temporally distinct outputs that peak and decline out of phase with one another, allowing for a sequence of different activities to be organized during signal processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of different effector dynamics.

claim: Simple point mutations to an effector can dramatically alter its output dynamics.
source: Finally, because even simple point mutations to an effector can dramatically alter its output dynamics, new dynamic patterns are not difficult to produce and can be easily accessed during evolution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing C-Raf N64A mutant behavior.

claim: Recruitment-based positive feedback was particularly effective at increasing output in high GAP network contexts.
source: Manual inspection of the curves from the system with or without feedback suggested that recruitment-feedback was particularly effective at increasing output in high GAP network contexts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Networks that contained high amounts of basal GAP-activity but only small amounts of input GEF showed the strongest differences in signal with recruitment-based feedback.
source: In particular, networks that contained high amounts of basal GAP-activity but only small amounts of input GEF showed the strongest differences in signal.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Allosteric feedback did not provide large gains in output amplitudes in any of the regimes examined.
source: Unlike with recruitment-based feedback, allosteric-feedback did not provide large gains in output amplitudes in any of the regimes we looked like.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Transient overshoot behavior was almost completely absent in the output responses of the SOScat system, even in the highest p120GAP condition.
source: However, we did observe that transient overshoot behavior was almost completely absent in the output responses of the SOScat system, even in the highest p120GAP condition we inspected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The output dynamics from allosteric-feedback networks appeared much more stable and monotonic than those from RasGRF networks that contained no feedback.
source: Indeed, the output dynamics from allosteric-feedback networks appeared much more stable and monotonic than those from RasGRF networks that contained no feedback.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing SOScat and RasGRF systems.

claim: For a RasGRF GEF step-input, the system experiences a sudden increase in catalytic activity all at once; for SOScat GEF, this step-input in protein levels becomes a ramp-input in terms of protein activity.
source: These differences in comparison to the RasGRF-RBD positive feedback system can be at least partially attributed to the OFF→ON feedback mechanism of SOScat in the context of a step-input: for a RasGRF GEF step-input, the system experiences a sudden increase in catalytic activity all at once; for SOScat GEF, although, this step-input in protein levels becomes a ramp-input in terms of protein activity because it takes multiple rounds of GEF activity to produce enough Ras•GTP for SOScat to achieve significant activity (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of SOScat activation, illustrated in Figure 8D.

claim: A single signaling system like Ras can encode multiple dynamic signal processing behaviors by regulating the concentration and identity of network components.
source: Our experiments imply that, much in the same way that a single genome can encode multiple cell types that are regulated through differential gene expression, a single signaling system like Ras can encode multiple dynamic signal processing behaviors by regulating the concentration and identity of network components.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of diverse outputs from different network configurations.

claim: There is a staggering amount of diversity in what types of network configurations are present in different cell types and tissues based on p120GAP, Ras, and c-Raf mRNA expression levels.
source: For example, a simple survey of published p120GAP, Ras, and c-Raf mRNA expression levels across a variety of tissue types reveals a staggering amount of diversity in what types of network configurations are present in different cell types and tissues (Figure 9A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data from Genevestigator shown in Figure 9A and Table 1.

claim: The versatility of Ras systems comes with a trade-off of fragility, as there exist numerous paths to altered signaling behaviors that could cause disease.
source: This versatility is not without trade-offs, however. In particular, we observed many different paths in network-space from one signaling processing behavior to another with much higher or sustained amplitude (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations, illustrated in Figure 9C.

claim: The same flexibility that allows Ras systems to realize many different signaling behaviors creates many opportunities for misregulation in response to perturbation.
source: Thus, the same flexibility that allows Ras systems to realize many different signaling behaviors creates many opportunities for misregulation in response to perturbation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of multiple paths to altered signaling.

claim: Network configurations that produced highly similar output behaviors could nonetheless respond divergently to perturbations.
source: Even networks configurations that produced highly similar output behaviors could nonetheless respond divergently to perturbations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of phase diagrams.

claim: Binding to activated Ras is a physiological prerequisite for other regulatory mechanisms to take place for Raf kinases.
source: However, this only further emphasizes the importance of effector binding dynamics in the context of cellular signal processing, as binding to Ras is a physiological prerequisite for these other mechanisms to take place.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Raf regulation.

claim: Intrinsic hydrolysis by H-Ras continues to occur even in the presence of saturating amounts of effector.
source: This result is consistent with previous observations that intrinsic hydrolysis by the GTPase continues to occur even in the presence of saturating amounts of effector (Herrmann et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The amount of nucleotide in solution is in vast excess of the small amount of bead-bound Ras present in the reactions, providing essentially an infinite supply of nucleotide for these reactions on the timescale examined.
source: This amount of nucleotide in solution is in vast excess of the small amount of bead-bound Ras present in the reactions, providing essentially an infinite supply of nucleotide for these reactions on the timescale we examine (detailed in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on calculation detailed in the methods section.

claim: NF1-GAP has a tight KM for Ras (0.3 μM) and modest kcat (1.4 s-1).
source: NF1-GAP, which is expressed somewhat ubiquitously but highest in neuronal cells and leukocytes, has a tight KM for Ras (0.3 μM) and modest kcat (1.4 s-1) (Wiesmüller and Wittinghofer, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published biochemical characterization.

claim: p120GAP has a higher KM (9.7 μM) for Ras and a higher kcat (19 s-1) compared to NF1-GAP.
source: In contrast, p120GAP has a higher KM (9.7 μM) for Ras, but also a higher kcat (19 s-1), and shows a much more ubiquitous expression profile (Wiesmüller and Wittinghofer, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published biochemical characterization.

claim: A-Raf has lower affinity for Ras•GTP (koff = 5.52x10-4 s-1, kon = 7.20x103 M-1s-1) than C-Raf (koff = 2.15x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.02x104 M-1s-1).
source: To this end, we purified and labeled RBDs from the A-Raf and B-Raf kinases, which have lower (koff = 5.52x10-4 s-1, kon = 7.20x103 M-1s-1) and higher (koff = 1.48x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.32x104 M-1s-1) affinities for Ras•GTP than C-Raf (koff = 2.15x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.02x104 M-1s-1), respectively (Fischer et al., 2007), to examine the signal processing behavior of two-effector systems in either GAP-free or high NF1-GAP networks.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published binding kinetics measurements.

claim: B-Raf has higher affinity for Ras•GTP (koff = 1.48x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.32x104 M-1s-1) than C-Raf (koff = 2.15x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.02x104 M-1s-1).
source: To this end, we purified and labeled RBDs from the A-Raf and B-Raf kinases, which have lower (koff = 5.52x10-4 s-1, kon = 7.20x103 M-1s-1) and higher (koff = 1.48x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.32x104 M-1s-1) affinities for Ras•GTP than C-Raf (koff = 2.15x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.02x104 M-1s-1), respectively (Fischer et al., 2007), to examine the signal processing behavior of two-effector systems in either GAP-free or high NF1-GAP networks.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published binding kinetics measurements.

claim: The catalytic domain from the RasGRF GEF is constitutively active and contains no allosteric feedback sites.
source: For our initial studies, we chose to use the catalytic domain from the RasGRF GEF, which is constitutively active and, unlike other GEFs, contains no allosteric feedback sites (Freedman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published characterization of RasGRF.

claim: SOScat has an intrinsic feedback mechanism such that the molecule has very low GEF activity in the absence of Ras•GTP, but Ras•GTP binding to a distal site on SOScat allosterically stimulates GEF activity to very high levels.
source: SOScat has an intrinsic feedback mechanism built in, such that the molecule has very low GEF activity in the absence of Ras•GTP, but Ras•GTP binding to a distal site on SOScat allosterically stimulates GEF activity to very high levels (Margarit et al., 2003; Freedman, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published structural and biochemical studies.

claim: In the absence of any GAP, effector fluorescence decayed with a rate constant of 0.01 min-1, which is similar to the expected rate of intrinsic hydrolysis by H-Ras under the assay conditions.
source: In the absence of any GAP, effector fluorescence decayed with a rate constant of 0.01 min-1, which is similar to the expected rate of intrinsic hydrolysis by H-Ras under our assay conditions (Neal et al., 1988; Gibbs et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to published kinetic measurements.

claim: When increasing amounts of NF1-GAP were included in the reactions, effector signal disappeared from the bead at an increased rate in a dose-dependent manner with a hyperbolic dependence on the GAP concentration.
source: When increasing amounts of the catalytic domain from purified Neurofibromin-1 GAP (NF1-GAP [Scheffzek et al., 1998; Xu et al., 1990]) were included in the reactions, effector signal disappeared from the bead at an increased rate in a dose-dependent manner with a hyperbolic dependence on the GAP concentration (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Initial rates of effector translocation showed a hyperbolic response to increasing GEF.
source: Initial rates of effector translocation appeared to show a hyperbolic response to increasing GEF, while steady states effector levels showed a linear response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Steady state effector levels showed a linear response to increasing GEF.
source: Initial rates of effector translocation appeared to show a hyperbolic response to increasing GEF, while steady states effector levels showed a linear response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.
